generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, slides often carry data: performance graphs, participation figures, outcome tables. The temptation is to put all of it on the screen and read it out. An effective visual aid does the opposite. It shows one clear graph or a few key words that support the point you are making aloud, so the audience follows your argument rather than decoding a crowded slide. A management student presenting participation data faces the same choice as a sport scientist with test results. The talk is your analysis; the slides serve it.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport management and development students design slides for the same presentation, a review of a community participation campaign.

Tom fills each slide with full paragraphs and every table of attendance figures, then reads them out word for word. The slides are crowded and hard to read from the back. The audience reads ahead and stops listening, and Tom runs over time. The slides have taken over the talk. This is the most common presentation error: the overloaded, read-aloud slide.

Amara puts only one clear graph or a few key words on each slide, enough to cue her point, and speaks around them. Her slides are easy to read and support what she says rather than repeating it. The audience listens, and the talk keeps to time. The slides help the argument instead of carrying it.

Both had the same campaign to present. Only Amara designed slides that support the talk rather than crowd it out.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, visual aids are there to support what you say, not to replace it. An effective slide is clear and uncluttered; the common errors, above all the overloaded slide read aloud, follow from forgetting that. You can now identify the features of an effective visual aid, tell a clear slide from an overloaded one, and recognise a common error and the move that avoids it. With what a presentation is, how to plan and structure one, and how to design its slides, you have the foundations to build a sport presentation of your own.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's slides better than Tom's?

items.text: She used one clear graph or a few key words to support each point, not full paragraphs and every table.
She used more slides than Tom did.
She used brighter colours on every slide.
She repeated her spoken words exactly on each slide.

feedback.correct: That's right. Spare slides that support the spoken point are the better design.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara's slides did with text and data.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's slides used one clear graph or a few key words to support each point. More slides, brighter colours or repeated text do not make a slide effective.
